recent_posts.title: The 2026 Junior Developer Trap
recent_posts.summary: AI tools in 2026 have created a paradox for junior developers: while seniors can use AI to multiply their output, juniors who rely on AI to write code risk never developing the deep technical foundation needed to become seniors. The job market increasingly demands senior-level skills, and companies adopting AI-first workflows need people who can catch AI mistakes. The advice is to use AI as a learning partner rather than a code generator — use it to understand data flow, debug reasoning, and explore approaches, but write the code yourself. Building strong fundamentals in architecture, system design, testing, and platform-specific concepts remains essential before leaning on AI tools.

Google Android CLI tool overview for AI agent driven development
recent_posts.summary: Google has released a new Android CLI tool that enables command-line control of Android Studio environments. Key capabilities include creating projects from templates, managing emulators, fetching official Android docs, capturing annotated screenshots, and extracting UI layout as JSON. The tool is particularly valuable for AI-first development workflows, allowing agents (like Claude or Codex) to interact with Android Studio programmatically with fewer tokens than GUI-based approaches. The 'android init' command installs agent skills, and 'android layout' provides JSON UI structure for automated verification. Annotated screenshots combined with 'android screen resolve' let agents identify and tap specific UI elements via ADB coordinates.

recent_posts.title: I've Tried the New Claude Design Tool to Create a PL Coding App
recent_posts.summary: A hands-on walkthrough of Claude Design, Anthropic's new AI-integrated design tool available at claude.ai/design. The author creates a design system by uploading brand assets (logo, fonts, color codes), iteratively refines typography, buttons, cards, and color palette through AI chat, then generates high-fidelity UI mockups for a mobile course members area app. Key observations include: the tool is more intuitive than using Claude Code with Figma MCP, supports granular AI-driven edits without regenerating entire screens, exports React/JSX code but lacks native mobile or Figma export, and currently skews toward web output. The author notes token usage is hidden from users and recommends the tool as a preferred design workflow going forward.

recent_posts.title: Beginner Course for AI-Assisted Android Development
recent_posts.summary: A beginner-level course demonstrating how to build a native Android habit tracking app using Claude Code as an AI coding assistant. The workflow covers setting up a CLAUDE.md system prompt file, configuring Android project dependencies via version catalog, creating a Jetpack Compose design system with custom fonts and colors, and designing a Room database schema through an interactive AI interview process. Key concepts include using plan mode before executing, managing context window limits, organizing project specs for AI reference, and maintaining developer oversight rather than blindly accepting AI output.

recent_posts.title: Three theoretical limits of LLMs that cannot be fixed
recent_posts.summary: A critical look at three fundamental, unfixable limitations of current LLM-based AI: (1) the learning ceiling problem — LLMs can't exceed the collective intelligence of their training data, especially as AI-generated content pollutes future training sets; (2) hallucination as an architectural inevitability — the same mechanism that enables creativity also produces confident incorrect outputs, and these can't be separated; (3) the frame problem — LLMs operate strictly within the context given to them and lack the ability to reframe a problem the way an experienced developer would. The author argues the truth lies between AI replacing developers and AI being useless, and that developers who understand these limits and use AI skillfully will gain a real productivity edge.

recent_posts.title: Why developers should stop chasing every new AI tool and pick one to master
recent_posts.summary: A measured take on AI hype in software development, arguing that the truth lies between extreme skepticism and uncritical belief in AI CEO predictions. Developers are encouraged to adopt one AI coding tool (Claude Code is personally recommended) and master it rather than chasing every new model or benchmark. AI is genuinely changing software development but is far from autonomously replacing developers, especially in complex enterprise contexts. The advice: engage with agentic coding workflows, but don't let FOMO drive anxiety-driven tool-hopping.

recent_posts.title: How attackers bypass Android in-app purchases and how to prevent it
recent_posts.summary: Android in-app purchases can be bypassed through two main attack vectors: static analysis via reverse engineering (using Jadx to read decompiled code and APKTool to modify and repackage the APK with smali edits) and dynamic instrumentation using Frida to hook and replace runtime function calls without modifying the APK. Both attacks work even against apps using the official Google Play Billing Library. Defenses include server-side purchase token validation (so premium state is never stored client-side) and advanced obfuscation tools like DexGuard, which applies control flow obfuscation, string encryption, and code virtualization — making decompilation ineffective and detecting Frida hooks or APK repackaging at runtime.

recent_posts.title: Will AI costs cause a bubble burst or just slower growth
recent_posts.summary: AI companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and big tech giants are burning massive amounts of capital in a race to build ever-larger models, with no clear path to profitability. However, the cost to achieve equivalent AI performance has dropped dramatically — GPT-3.5-level performance fell from $20 to $0.07 per million tokens in just two years, a 285x reduction. The argument is that cost alone won't burst the AI bubble; instead, growth will likely slow as training costs hit a ceiling, consolidating the market to two or three dominant players. The analogy to the dot-com bubble is explored: like the internet, AI's underlying business value is real and unlikely to disappear, but the hype cycle may cool into slower, steadier growth.
